This file lists what is **decided** about how the chip panel is assembled, and what is still
**open**. Every open item says what the MVP does in the meantime, so the code can be built and
the decision taken later without rebuilding anything. Numbers marked *measured* come from the
test runs `test_region_2026-10-19` (subregion 2, zone 20) and `test_region_para_2026-10-19`
(subregion 4, zone 21). Reasoning in more depth: `code/panel_assembly_strategy.md`.

# Decided principles

| # | Principle | Consequence |
|---|---|---|
| P1 | **The panel is complete.** Every planned chip has a row in every period. Nothing is deleted or filtered out. | A chip whose tile failed keeps its row, with `scored = FALSE` and missing scores. "No data" is never "no mine". |
| P2 | **The panel is additive.** Later steps only add variables, flags and statistics. They never change or remove what is already there. | Persistence, isolation, SAM2 and any better rule later are extra columns (flags), not filters. |
| P3 | **Monthly and quarterly are separate panels** with the same `chip_id`. | Separate folders. The monthly panel can be joined to its quarter in one line through the quarter tag. |
| P4 | **One run at a time.** A run is one `plan.py` result: one chip list, one frozen config, one model. | The cluster parallelises *inside* a run, by period and subregion. Assembly reads all of a run's task folders. |
| P5 | **Two assembly scripts, split by axis.** `assemble_period.py` works on one period across space; `build_panel.py` works on one area across time. | Neither ever needs the whole panel in memory. |
| P6 | **pandas and pyarrow** for now. | DuckDB is an open choice in the cluster migration notes (D10). |

# Open design decisions

| # | Topic | MVP does |
|---|---|---|
| D1 | Isolation rule depends on cloud cover | AMW's flags, plus the distance and `n_clear` stored |
| D2 | Chips near the edge of the scored area look isolated | Nothing yet |
| D3 | How distances are measured | Both measures stored; flags use AMW's |
| D4 | One mine fires a blob of overlapping chips | Nothing yet |
| D5 | UTM zone seams are scored twice | Both copies kept |
| D6 | Unit of analysis: chips or 240 m cells | Chip panel only; 240 m cells proposed |
| D7 | Border tiles listed in two subregions | Refuses the period, with a message |
| D8 | Persistence rule | Not built yet; will be a flag |
| D9 | Last day of each period | Our convention (last day included) |
| D10 | DuckDB or pandas/pyarrow | pandas/pyarrow |
| D11 | Storage when nothing is deleted | Keep everything |
| D12 | Combining several runs | Not supported |
| D13 | How added variables are stored | One file per layer and period, identical rows |

## D1. The isolation rule depends on cloud cover

AMW's dual threshold makes a chip with confidence ≥ `t_main` that is *isolated* (its 5th nearest
detected neighbour is more than 3 km away) also clear the stricter `t_iso`. Fewer clear images
mean fewer detections, so fewer neighbours, so more isolated chips.

*Measured*, Pará run: in 2026Q1 (mean `n_clear` 4.9) **27 of 51** catalogue chips are isolated;
in 2026Q2 (`n_clear` 19.5) **1 of 701**. So `det_loose` partly measures weather.

**MVP:** AMW's flags, and the 5th-neighbour distance and the image counts in every row, so a
better rule can be derived later from the stored columns.

## D2. Edges look isolated

A chip near the edge of the scored area has neighbours on one side only. *Measured:* in the test
region 2026Q1, 4 of the 14 isolated chips are within 3 km of the test area's edge. In the full run
this only happens at Amazon_ACA's outer border; in every test run it happens everywhere.

**Options:** a `near_edge` flag; ignore it; drop the rule at the border. **MVP:** nothing yet, and
isolation statistics from test runs are not representative.

## D3. How distances are measured

AMW measures the 3 km in one UTM zone: `postprocess.centroids_xy_m` calls geopandas'
`estimate_utm_crs()`, which picks the single zone at the centre of the data's bounding box. AMW
runs it on the whole basin per period, which gives zone 20S for all of Amazon_ACA (79.6°W to
43.7°W, seven zones). UTM stretches distances away from the zone's central meridian (63°W).

*Measured* with pyproj, a true 3 km reads as:

| Longitude | 80°W | 75°W | 70°W | 63°W | 55°W | 50°W | 45°W |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| AMW's distance | 3.135 km | 3.066 | 3.021 | 2.999 | 3.028 | 3.078 | 3.153 |

So at the western and eastern ends a chip is called isolated about 4–5% too early. Madre de Dios
(~70°W) is off by ~0.7%, the Tapajós (~56°W) by ~2–3%, Ecuador and Colombia (~77°W) by ~4%.

**Why AMW doesn't correct it (what the code and history show):**

- The rule was "codified from the notebook workflow" in commit `5d11b6b` (2 Jun 2026), written
  with an AI coding assistant. Nothing in their code, docs or published config discusses the
  projection; their public config lists only `k = 5` and `isolation_km = 3.0`.
- Their evaluation notebook (`fd1231e`) says they project everything into "one shared metric CRS
  (from the catalog), so distances stay meaningful across geographic splits". So they cared that
  all chips use the *same* measure, not that the measure is *accurate*.
- They tuned only `t_iso` (a sweep against known mining and non-mining regions); `k = 5` and 3 km
  were fixed. The rule is described as "a simple spatial prior" on their blog. A heuristic with an
  untuned 3 km cut-off makes a 5% error look unimportant.
- They know great-circle (haversine) distances: they use them elsewhere (commit `99f944a`).

Our reading: not a deliberate choice, rather a convenient default whose error nobody measured.

**Options:** (a) AMW exactly, comparable with their product; (b) great-circle distances, correct
everywhere; (c) store both. Note that on a small test run (a)'s zone is the run's own zone, so
(a) only differs from (b) on the full run. **MVP:** (c), with the flags computed from (a).

## D4. One mine fires a blob of chips

Chips overlap four times (24 px stride), so one scar lights up a 2×2 or larger block, and a chip's
5th "neighbour" is often part of the same scar. *Measured:* 31–61% of catalogue chips have their
5th neighbour less than 0.5 km away. The rule then mostly measures blob size, not whether mines
cluster. **MVP:** AMW's rule as it is.

## D5. UTM zone seams are scored twice

Each zone's tile grid runs ~4.5 km past the zone line, so a ~9 km strip at every seam enters the
panel twice, on two unrelated grids, with different keys and different centres. Neither our
chip_id dedupe nor AMW's centroid dedupe catches it. *Measured* at 66°W, 11–12°S: 183
cross-zone tile pairs overlap, median 3.3%, max 81% of a tile. Amazon_ACA spans 7 zones (17–23).

**Proposed rule:** keep a cell (or chip) only if its centre lies inside its own zone's 6° band.
**MVP:** both copies kept. Whatever rule is chosen becomes a column of the chip table, so no
assembly code has to change.

## D6. Unit of analysis: overlapping chips or non-overlapping cells

*Measured* 19 Oct from the code (`core/tile_utils.py`, `core/gee.py`, `lib/grid.py`), not from
comments, with `checks/overlap/overlap.py` and `tiles.py` (areas in EPSG:6933, equal-area). Ruby,
23 Oct: the analysis level is not known yet (municipality, a border buffer, ...); the aim is to
measure how mining **grows**, so the panel needs counts or areas at a fine spatial level.

**How the geometry is built.**

1. `DLTile.iter_from_shape(region, tilesize=552, pad=12, resolution=10)` lays UTM squares on a
   fixed grid, one per UTM zone. Tile key = `552:12:10.0:zone:ti:tj`.
2. `get_tile_data` (gee.py) does not download the UTM square. It takes the lon/lat bounding box
   of the reprojected, slightly tilted square and asks for 576 × 576 pixels filling it. So every
   tile has its own lat/lon pixel grid, slightly bigger than the square.
3. `cut_chips` slides a 48 px window in 24 px steps: 23 × 23 = 529 chips, column-major. Chip
   polygons are interpolated from the same box, so the polygon in `chips.parquet` is exactly the
   footprint the model saw.

**What overlaps** (*measured*):

| Level | Overlap? | Kind | Size |
|---|---|---|---|
| Subregions 1–6 | no | | largest pairwise intersection 0.0 |
| Tiles on subregion borders | same tile twice | side effect (6 separate jobs) | 1,186 of 274,932 tiles (0.43%), 1 tile three times; same key, so dedupe on chip_id is exact (D7) |
| Neighbouring tiles, padding | yes | by design (`pad: 12`) | a 24 px shared strip, median 4.2% of a tile per pair; tiling covers its area 1.093 times (Madre de Dios) |
| Neighbouring tiles, projection | yes | side effect (lat/lon box of a tilted square) | even with pad 0: median 0.35%, max 0.70% per pair |
| UTM zone seams | yes, large | side effect | D5 |
| Chips inside a tile | ×4 | by design (stride 24) | chip area / union = 3.99 (La Pampa), 4.01 (Madre de Dios) |
| "Every other chip" | almost disjoint | side effect (projection) | 0 inside a tile; across tile edges 29–31% of the subset overlaps a neighbour by up to 7.5% of a chip; ~0.7% of area counted twice. So the 8 Oct claim of an "exact 480 m grid" is wrong, and it would discard 75% of the scores |

Chip area is 231,666–233,666 m², not 230,400, because the pixels sit on a lat/lon grid.

**Why the overlaps by design exist.** The 24 px stride means anything up to 240 m across fits
whole inside at least one chip; without it a mine on a chip edge is cut in two and each half may
be too small to detect. The padding makes the chips of neighbouring tiles continue one seamless
24 px lattice (chip offsets run `24 × (23·ti + j) − 12` across tile edges). The projection
slivers and the zone seams have no purpose; both can be removed by a rule.

**Why it matters for growth.** A chip is 2 × 2 blocks of 240 m. A mine covering k × k blocks
touches (k+1)² = k² + 2k + 1 chips: area plus perimeter plus one. A mine growing from 1 to
2 × 2 blocks grows ×4 in area but from 4 to 9 chips, ×2.25. Chip counts understate the growth
of expanding mines and overstate the size of small ones: a bias with a known sign, not noise.
(In practice the detector won't fire on every touching chip, but the structure stays.)

**The proposal: a 240 m cell lattice for analysis, chips stay the measurement.** The stride
lattice already partitions space. Cut each padded tile into 24 × 24 blocks of 24 px; block 23 of
tile i is the same ground as block 0 of tile i+1 (the padding), so keep blocks 1–23: 529 cells
per tile, one per chip, an exact partition in UTM within a zone. Each interior cell lies under
exactly 4 chip windows (two may belong to the neighbouring tile). The cell's value is a function
of those 4 scores (mean, max, any above the threshold), or of the SAM2 mask pixels inside it,
which then sum correctly because no pixel is counted twice. Each cell has one centre, so it
belongs to exactly one municipality or buffer and aggregates up exactly. Zone seams: D5's rule.

**Objections.** It doesn't remove spatial dependence, it gives it a known form: neighbouring
cells share 2 of their 4 chips, so a cell outcome is a 2 × 2 moving average by construction.
Standard errors must still be clustered (tile) or Conley. If the regressors vary at municipality
level, the effective N is the number of municipalities, not billions of rows. And growth rates
will differ by aggregation level (the modifiable areal unit problem); that is chosen with the
research question.

**Still to answer:** the main regressors and their spatial level; the exact SAM2 idea; whether
the outcome is the score, a 0/1 detection or mined area.

**MVP:** the chip panel, every score kept. A cell layer would be a later, separate step built
from the stored chip scores, with no new Earth Engine requests.

## D7. Border tiles

A tile on a subregion border is listed under both subregions and scored twice, under the same
`chip_id`. AMW keeps the copy with the higher confidence. Under P1 we could instead keep both with a
flag. **MVP:** none of the test runs has border tiles; `assemble_period.py` refuses a period
in which a chip was scored twice, with a message naming this decision. To be built once a run
with border tiles exists.

## D8. Persistence rule

Calendar version (a detection in year Y and again in Y+1, closest to AMW), rolling version (2
detections within 12 months), or adding annual composites (~6% more Earth Engine requests, copies
AMW exactly). Whatever is chosen is a flag (P2). Needs more than one year of data to test.

## D9. Last day of each period

Our periods end on the 1st of the next period, which Earth Engine excludes, so every day is in.
AMW passes the period's last day as the (excluded) end, so 31 Mar, 30 Jun, 30 Sep and 31 Dec are
never imaged. *Measured* (`amw_comparison/last_day_check.ipynb`), Pará 2026Q1: 56 detections ours
against 27 AMW's, and the whole gap is 31 March. AMW's own code reproduces both results exactly
with the two end dates.

**For ours:** whole calendar periods, and three months add up exactly to their quarter
(`n_obs`, `n_clear`; *measured* exact on 57,132 chip-quarters). **For AMW's:** direct
comparability with their published product. **MVP:** ours.

## D10. DuckDB or pandas/pyarrow

DuckDB reads Parquet, sorts and joins bigger-than-memory tables, and computes per-chip time
variables in SQL. pandas/pyarrow is what we know. Moved to the cluster migration notes.
**MVP:** pandas/pyarrow.

## D11. Storage when nothing is deleted

The earlier plan deleted detect's part files once a period was assembled. With nothing deleted,
the part files (~0.8 TB *estimate*) stay next to the assembled panel (about the same again, plus
the added layers). Goethe's `/work` has a 5 TB *group* quota and no backup. **Options:** keep
everything on `/work`; move part files to the archive after checks; delete them after a verified
copy. **MVP:** keep everything.

## D12. Combining several runs

Not needed if the whole region is one run (P4). If it ever is (for example, a later extension),
assembly would need the runs' frozen scoring settings and model fingerprints to be identical.
**MVP:** not supported.

## D13. How added variables are stored

Rewriting a ~1 TB panel to add one column is slow and risky. Proposed: each step writes its own
**layer**: one file per period, with exactly the same rows in the same order (every planned chip,
sorted by `chip_id`). Adding a variable means adding a layer and never touching an existing one;
reading puts the layers side by side. Time-invariant chip attributes (tile, `in_andes`, square)
stay once in `plan/chips.parquet`, not repeated in every period. **MVP:** two layers,
`scores` (detect's values) and `postprocess` (AMW's flags and distances).

Added 23 Oct 2026 so that no open item lives only in an archived note. The letters are the
item numbers of the 19 Oct review (`history/quarterly_and_parallel_runs.md` §6) and of the

| # | Topic | Now | Proposal |
|---|---|---|---|

| L4 (D4) | Quarterly first? | Order is monthly, then quarterly (Ruby, 8 Oct) | Quarterly is a third of the requests and less cloudy; with L1 binding, a complete quarterly panel first may be worth more |
| L5 (D5) | GPU for scoring | CPU only | Not needed while Earth Engine is the limit (R2); one test job if that changes |
| L6 (C5) | A task longer than the job time limit | Resubmitting resumes it | Fine as is; tile shards only if it becomes a nuisance |
| L7 (A1) | `--run` is resolved from the current folder, config paths from the repository root | Run every command from the repository root | Resolve a relative `--run` from the repository root |
| L8 (A5) | Hive partition columns come back as text | `lib/read_panel.py` and the notebook set the types | Keep doing so in every reader |
| L9 (A6) | A moved run folder keeps its old `output_root` in the frozen config | Harmless | Check the folder name against `run.name` |
| L10 (B2) | No dry run | | `--dry-run`: print periods, tiles, folders and their state, stop before the Earth Engine login |
| L11 (B3) | `--from 2026-01` with quarterly is refused | Refused | Say "did you mean 2026Q1?" |
| L12 (B5) | A cloud-wrecked period looks complete | | Print the period's mean `n_clear` and `empty_share` in its closing log line |
